items_missed: Availability for the move date never checked. She confirmed Tuesday, September 29th off the profile but never told the customer we have it open.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener — 'let me explain how our pricing works' is functional but drops the simplicity frame, which mattered on a call that opened with a price objection.

Quote is not accurate for the job described — see the coaching note. She quoted 3.5 to 4.5 hours and $714–$918 on a move the customer described as pre-packed, staged in the garage, four items upstairs, park out front at both ends, fifteen minutes apart.

No typical time range for the home size was ever given. She jumped straight to the job-specific number with no benchmark, which is why her defense of it collapsed — when the customer pushed back, 'just with the items eleven, I estimate it three hours but since there is a stairs involved on both apartment. I added time for the staircase access' had nothing underneath it. With no stated benchmark, 'I added time' sounds like a number she chose rather than a number she derived.
Drive time never factored or mentioned, despite the customer volunteering 'The properties are about fifteen minutes apart, drive time.' He handed her the number and it never appeared in the estimate.

Walk distance never asked. She asked about parking at both ends and got 'yes' twice, but never converted that into a carry distance — and 'park right out front, everything is staged in the garage' is precisely the fact that should have pushed the estimate down.
Traffic never mentioned as a variable on a Tuesday Grapevine-to-Irving run.
Assembly and disassembly never discussed as a time variable, on a move with a bed and two couches.
No equivalents or plain-language anchors used to make three-and-a-half-to-four-and-a-half hours feel earned rather than asserted.

Save Your Ass entirely absent — 0/10, and uniquely costly here because the customer had already done it himself. 'Everything is already pre packed and staged in the garage' and 'I'm probably gonna do a lot of a small stuff myself, I just need help with the big items really' is the customer reciting the Save Your Ass speech back to her, unprompted. She never acknowledged it, never praised it, and never credited it in the estimate.
Zero booking attempt. She never asked for the date, never offered to hold it, never asked what would need to be true to move forward.

No deposit required was never mentioned — the highest-cost single omission on this call. The objection was 'that's too much money,' and 'there's no deposit and no card on file, so holding the date costs you nothing' is the one answer that keeps a price-objecting customer in the funnel.
No email handoff of any kind. She never offered to send the estimate, never confirmed his email, and never gave him anything to compare against other companies. He hung up with nothing in writing.
BOLDED-details framing and the 'reply with any corrections' ask both absent — there was no email at all.
No 'any other questions before I let you go?' — after the objection she went straight to 'Thank you so for your time. Bye for now.'
Hours and how to reach us never given.

Customer's mood declined over the call. He arrived believing the online quote was too high and left saying 'I might just move myself that's too much money' — the politeness bullet on mood is a clear miss.
Customer's name used once, and garbled ('thank you ison'). He had spelled it out letter by letter — 'E-A-S-T-O-N-S-C-O-T-T' — and it was never said cleanly again.

The washer/dryer shipping-bolt exchange was pushed past three explicit disengagement signals. 'I don't know why that would even matter,' 'It's a strange question,' and 'I'm not worried about it at all is your concern' — and she continued, including suggesting he go buy shipping bolts. That is roughly ninety seconds spent on a $0 item while a price-sensitive customer cooled off.
top_strength: Nicole runs the best front two-thirds of any call in this batch, and it is not close. Her discovery is a clean 9/9 — the only perfect Probe section this week — and it is thorough in a way that shows real product knowledge rather than list-reading. She asked the stressor question first, before anything else, and phrased it better than the rubric does: 'let's talk about your move first. What are your biggest concerns and what are the most important things you want answers to on this call today?' She probed heavy items with a specific threshold ('anything that's like more than £400'), asked about art and antiques and collections, asked about additional stops, and asked about parking at both ends separately. And the washer/dryer question is genuine expertise: 'your washer and dryer, are they front load or top load?... front loads are fragile during moving process, they usually requires to have a shipping bolts. Do you still have the shipping bolts for the dryer, the four big screws?' That is a rep who knows what actually breaks on a move day. Her agenda is one of only two clean agenda_opener hits this week, and she used it to reframe the customer's own objection before he could harden it: 'the estimate you got online, it just based on the size of your apartment. But don't worries since you have me on the line I'll be giving you an accurate estimate, I just need about ten to fifteen minutes will that be fine?' Purpose, contrast with the instant quote, timeframe and confirmation — and it turned 'I thought the quote was really high' into a reason to stay on the phone. Her Pricing section is the best in the batch at 18/20, and she is the only rep of the eight to deliver all three differentiators, each word-perfect: 'we have no worries, damage coverage, we provide up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace or reimburse for any accidental damages,' then Meet Your Mover including the reason it exists — 'you will have an option to see their photos and basic info just helping [with the apprehension] of strangers arriving at your front door' — then On-Time Guarantee: 'if we cannot make it in the time window that we arrange we immediately start discounting money of your final bill.' Her Clock is a clean 4/4 including the on-site contract-open trigger and a sense-check. Through minute seven, this is a 77-plus call.
coaching_note: This is the most instructive call of the week and it belongs in the bottom-4 review file as the primary exhibit. Nicole did everything right for seven minutes — perfect discovery, all three differentiators, perfect clock, the best agenda in the batch — and then lost the sale in a single sentence by padding the estimate. Estimate-accuracy flag, and it is the clearest one this week. The customer did her job for her. Unprompted, in his first substantive answer, he said: 'It should only take like three hours to complete the entire move. The properties are about fifteen minutes apart, drive time and pretty much everything is already pre packed and staged in the garage. They, the movers it only need to go upstairs to pick up like a mattress and like one mattress and two couches and like one cabinet.' Then he added less than twenty boxes, and that the washer, dryer and fridge are already downstairs in the garage. Then he confirmed we can park right in front at both ends. Every single one of those facts pushes the number down. Four items upstairs at origin; everything else at truck level; a fifteen-minute haul; park out front at both ends. Nicole quoted 3.5 to 4.5 hours and $714 to $918, and justified it with 'since there is a stairs involved on both apartment. I added time for the staircase access.' But the stairs only apply to four items, and she never subtracted anything for the staging that eliminated stairs for everything else. The customer's response was immediate and final: 'Yeah, I'm not interested. That's too, that's too much. It shouldn't take that long.' This is the apartment version of the padding pattern — not fear of a bad big-move experience, but reflexively adding hours for a variable that was already neutralized by the customer's own prep. What she should have said: 'Based on what you've told me, you've already done the two things that make a move fast — everything's packed and everything heavy is already staged in the garage. So I'd put this at the minimum to three hours, call it $510 to $612, and we only bill for the time we actually use. The only thing that could push it is the four items still upstairs.' That number is defensible, it is probably closer to the truth, and it books. Second lesson, and it is the reason the padding was fatal rather than survivable: she had no benchmark. She never said what a two-bedroom typically takes. So when the customer pushed back, she had nothing to stand on — 'I estimate it three hours but since there is a stairs involved I added time' is an admission that she moved the number by feel. Always state the typical range first, then adjust with named facts, in both directions. Third: after the objection, she folded instantly. One restatement of her math, and then 'I see. Thank you so for your time. Bye for now.' No no-deposit, no offer to send anything in writing, no request to keep the date, no attempt to re-scope the job at a lower number. A customer who says 'I might just move myself' is not gone — he is negotiating. At minimum: 'Let me at least send this to you in writing so you have it, and here's the thing — there's no deposit and no card on file. Holding the twenty-ninth costs you nothing and you can cancel any time.' She ended this call with zero in Section 7, which is a rep who did eight minutes of excellent work and captured none of it. Fourth, read the room. The shipping-bolt thread ran past three explicit brush-offs — 'I don't know why that would even matter,' 'It's a strange question,' 'I'm not worried about it at all' — and she kept going, to the point of suggesting he buy shipping bolts. The knowledge is a genuine asset; the persistence spent it. When a customer disengages twice on a detail, note it in the file, say 'no problem at all, I'll flag it for the crew,' and move on. Those ninety seconds were the ones she needed for the Save Your Ass speech and the close.
phone_presence_notes: Warm on the surface and clearly trying — 'Okay, awesome,' 'Okay, great,' 'good to hear that,' and a genuine thank-you for the details — but the affirmations run on a loop of roughly ten near-identical 'okay great/awesome's that stop reading as responses, and the warmth failed at the two moments it was needed: she pushed the shipping-bolt question past three explicit brush-offs, and when the customer objected on price she answered with arithmetic rather than acknowledgment and let him leave on 'I might just move myself.'
audio_review_reason: A 3 on a call that ended with a lost customer, and the two decisive moments are exactly the ones transcripts render worst. The shipping-bolt exchange reads on paper as a rep not listening, but it could equally be a rep sounding genuinely helpful about a real risk — those produce identical text and opposite coaching. More importantly, the price objection at the end needs ears: whether 'I see, actually, just with the items eleven, I estimate it three hours but since there is a stairs involved' was delivered with any warmth, apology or flexibility in the voice, or flatly as a restatement, determines whether this is a tone problem or purely a pricing-judgment problem. Given her scorecard is otherwise near-mastery through minute seven, getting that diagnosis right matters.
